questions.q: Ananya says: 'A metal vein lying 8 km under a mountain, beyond the reach of every drill, is a resource today, because it is valuable to humans.' Is she right? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. She is right that the vein occurs in Nature and is valuable to humans, which is the chapter's short definition. But for an entity to be called a resource it must also be technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable, all together. A vein beyond every drill fails the technology condition, so it is not a resource today.
s: Verdict: no
What she has right: it occurs in Nature and is valuable to humans
The failing condition: technological accessibility, and all three conditions must hold

questions.q:
Riya says, 'The plastic button on my shirt is made in a factory, so it has nothing to do with Nature.'
(a) What does the chapter say about where the origin of such an object leads?
(b) Using (a), is the button itself a natural resource? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Followed back, the origin of every object around us leads to Nature at some point, even the plastic button. (b) No. Natural resources are materials and substances that occur in Nature; the button was made by humans. Nature is where its origin leads, but the finished button is not itself a natural resource.
s: Part (a): every object's origin leads back to Nature, even the plastic button
Part (b): the button is not itself a natural resource, since it was made by humans and does not occur in Nature

questions.q: Four sentences use the word 'exploitation'. Which one uses it in the sense this chapter gives it?
questions.a: The farmers' exploitation of the canal water to grow wheat. The chapter uses 'exploitation' to mean the extraction, utilisation and consumption of natural resources, with no negative sense. The other three use the everyday sense of unfair or harmful use, or are not about a natural resource at all.
o: The farmers' exploitation of the canal water to grow wheat
The owner's exploitation of workers by paying them too little
The cheat's exploitation of a gap in the shop's billing rules
The bully's exploitation of a younger child's fear of the dark

questions.q: A class is asked to pick the one item below that is part of Nature in the chapter's sense, that is, not created by humans. Which should a careful student choose?
questions.a: A banyan sapling that seeded itself in a crack of an old wall. Nobody planted it. The canal, the bamboo fence and the tank were each made by people, though what they hold or are made of came from Nature.
o: A banyan sapling that seeded itself in a crack of an old wall
A canal dug by farmers to carry river water to their fields
A fence of cut bamboo poles put up by the school gardener
A tank dug by the village to store rain for the dry months

questions.q:
A jeweller in Jaipur buys gold dug from a working mine in Karnataka. On a farmer's hillside in Bihar the same metal lies in small amounts; his tools can reach it and no one objects, but digging costs Rs 9,000 for each gram while gold sells for Rs 6,000 a gram.
(a) Which of the two golds is a resource in the chapter's sense?
(b) Using (a), the price of gold rises to Rs 12,000 a gram while the digging cost stays the same. Which condition changes for the hillside gold, and why do the other two conditions stay as they were?
questions.a: (a) The mined gold the jeweller buys. (b) Economic feasibility changes: at Rs 12,000 a gram the gold now sells for Rs 3,000 more than it costs to dig. A price rise does not alter the farmer's tools or what the community accepts, so technological accessibility and cultural acceptability are unchanged; all three now hold.
s: Part (a): the mined gold is the resource
Part (b): economic feasibility changes, with the Rs 3,000 margin; technology and culture are unaffected by price

questions.q:
A district survey in Jharkhand (illustrative) lists four finds:
P. A coal seam near the surface; machines are available, coal sells for more than it costs to dig, and the land is not sacred.
Q. Iron ore under a hill that the local community worships; mining would be cheap and machines are available.
R. A thin seam of copper so deep that no available machine can reach it.
S. A river that farmers already use for irrigation through channels they built.
(a)-(d) For each find, decide whether it is a resource now and, if not, name the condition that fails.
(e) A new deep-mining machine is bought next year. Which find could change its status, and why only that one?
questions.a: (a) P: a resource; all three conditions hold. (b) Q: not a resource; it is technologically accessible and economically feasible, but mining a worshipped hill is not culturally acceptable. (c) R: not a resource; it is not technologically accessible. (d) S: a resource; the water is used and meets all three conditions. (e) R, because only R was held back by technology. The machine could make it accessible, though it would then also have to be worth its cost. A machine cannot change Q's status, since Q fails on culture, not technology.
s: Part (a): P is a resource, all three hold
Part (b): Q fails cultural acceptability
Part (c): R fails technological accessibility
Part (d): S is a resource
Part (e): only R, since only R failed on technology, and it must still be economic

questions.q:
(a) Why does the chapter add a note on the meaning of the word 'exploitation'?
(b) Using (a), how might a reader misread the sentence 'Our state's exploitation of its coal has grown' without that note?
questions.a: (a) Usually the word has a negative connotation, but the chapter uses it to mean only the extraction, utilisation and consumption of natural resources. (b) Without the note, the reader could take the sentence as saying the state is misusing or harming its coal unfairly, when it says only that the state is mining and using more coal.
s: Part (a): usual negative sense against the chapter's neutral meaning
Part (b): the reader would wrongly read misuse into a sentence about extraction and use

questions.q:
An oil field lies 3,200 m below the seabed off the Gujarat coast (illustrative figures). The fishing community nearby has no objection to drilling.
| Year | Deepest reach of drills | Cost to extract one barrel | Selling price of one barrel |
| 2018 | 2,500 m | not known | Rs 6,000 |
| 2021 | 3,500 m | Rs 7,500 | Rs 6,000 |
| 2024 | 3,500 m | Rs 5,200 | Rs 6,200 |
(a) In 2018, which condition kept the oil from being a resource?
(b) In 2021, which condition failed, and by how much per barrel?
(c) Was the oil a resource in 2024? Show the working.
(d) In 2027 the selling price falls to Rs 5,000 a barrel while the cost stays at Rs 5,200 and the drills are unchanged. Predict the oil's status in 2027 and name the condition that decides it.
questions.a: (a) Technological accessibility: the oil is at 3,200 m but drills reached only 2,500 m. (b) Economic feasibility: drills could now reach 3,500 m, but each barrel cost Rs 7,500 - Rs 6,000 = Rs 1,500 more to extract than it sold for. (c) Yes: drills reach it, the price exceeds the cost by Rs 6,200 - Rs 5,200 = Rs 1,000 a barrel, and there is no cultural objection, so all three conditions hold. (d) Not a resource in 2027: drills reach it and nobody objects, but each barrel now costs Rs 5,200 - Rs 5,000 = Rs 200 more than it sells for, so economic feasibility fails. A resource can stop being one when conditions change, just as the oil became one earlier.
s: Part (a): technology, 2,500 m reach against 3,200 m depth
Part (b): economic feasibility, a loss of Rs 1,500 a barrel
Part (c): yes, Rs 1,000 margin and all three conditions met
Part (d): not a resource in 2027; a Rs 200 loss a barrel fails economic feasibility

questions.q:
Two villages in Odisha, Marigaon and Nilgiripada (illustrative), stand on identical bauxite hills. A company can reach the bauxite in both with machines it already owns, and mining would earn Rs 2,500 a tonne over cost in each. Marigaon's people agreed to mining; Nilgiripada's people worship their hill and refused.
(a) Is the bauxite of each village a resource in the chapter's sense?
(b) The hills, machines and profit are identical. Which one condition explains the difference?
(c) The company raises its offer to Rs 5,000 a tonne over cost for Nilgiripada. Does that change the status of its bauxite? Explain with the three conditions.
(d) Predict what happens to the status of Nilgiripada's bauxite if, years later, its community decides on its own that mining is acceptable.
questions.a: (a) Marigaon's bauxite is a resource; Nilgiripada's is not. (b) Cultural acceptability: it is the only condition that differs. (c) No. A bigger profit strengthens only economic feasibility, which already held; the cultural condition still fails, and all three must hold. (d) It would become a resource, because technological accessibility, economic feasibility and cultural acceptability would then all hold.
s: Part (a): Marigaon yes, Nilgiripada no
Part (b): cultural acceptability
Part (c): no, money affects only the economic condition and all three are needed
Part (d): it becomes a resource once all three hold

questions.q: 'An element of Nature becomes a resource only through human eyes.' Justify this statement using the chapter's meaning of Nature, its definition of natural resources and its three conditions.
questions.a: (1) Nature is all life and non-life forms in our environment that humans did not create; it exists whether or not anyone uses it. (2) Natural resources are materials and substances that occur in Nature and are valuable to humans; a tree becomes a resource when its wood is cut and made into furniture. (3) Technological accessibility depends on human ability: petroleum deep under the ocean cannot be reached without the technology. (4) Economic feasibility depends on human cost: extraction that costs too much does not make a resource. (5) Cultural acceptability depends on human values: trees in sacred groves are not cut. Each test is about human use, ability, cost or values, which justifies the statement.
s: Nature exists independently of humans
Definition: valuable to humans, used to make things, tree and furniture
Technological accessibility depends on human ability
Economic feasibility depends on human cost
Cultural acceptability depends on human values, sacred groves

questions.q: True or False? 'Anything that occurs in Nature is a natural resource.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Natural resources are materials and substances that occur in Nature AND are valuable to humans; and to be called a resource an element must also be technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable. Petroleum beyond the reach of any drill occurs in Nature but is not yet a resource.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it must also be valuable to humans and meet the three conditions, with an example

questions.q: A metal ore lies so deep under a mountain that no machine yet built can reach it, although buyers would pay well for it and nobody objects to mining there. The one condition it fails is ___ accessibility.
questions.a: technological

questions.q:
Pond P lies deep in a forest where no one lives. Pond Q, of the same size, supplies water to a village in Bundelkhand.
(a) Using the chapter's meaning of the words, which pond is only part of Nature and which is a resource?
(b) Using (a), explain whether the difference lies in the ponds themselves or somewhere else.
questions.a: (a) Pond P is part of Nature; Pond Q is a resource. (b) The difference is not in the ponds, which are alike; it lies in human use. An element of Nature becomes a resource when humans use it for their sustenance, as the village does with Pond Q, just as a tree becomes a resource when its wood is turned into furniture.
s: Part (a): P is Nature only, Q is a resource
Part (b): the difference is human use, not the pond itself

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the description in Column B that fits it.
Column A: 1. A coal seam beneath a town that would cost more to mine than the coal would fetch  2. Old trees in a grove the community holds sacred  3. Petroleum under the deep ocean, beyond the reach of any drill  4. A stream whose water a village leads to its fields through a cheap channel it built
Column B: a. not culturally acceptable  b. meets all three conditions, so a resource  c. not economically feasible  d. not technologically accessible
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. The coal seam fails on cost (economic); the sacred grove fails on culture; the deep-ocean petroleum cannot be reached (technology); the stream is reached, cheap to use and acceptable, so it is a resource.

questions.q: An exploration team finds petroleum below the seabed off the Gujarat coast. Its rigs can reach the oil, and no one nearby objects, but extracting each barrel would cost more than the barrel sells for. In the chapter's terms, why is this oil not yet a resource?
questions.a: Its extraction is not economically feasible. The rigs can reach it, so it is technologically accessible, and no one objects, so it is culturally acceptable; the cost being higher than the price is the economic condition failing. Oil under the seabed is still part of Nature, because humans did not create it.
o: Its extraction is not economically feasible
It is not technologically accessible yet
Its use is not culturally acceptable
Oil lying under the seabed is not a part of Nature

questions.q: A timber merchant offers a village in Meghalaya a good price for the trees of its sacred grove. A road already reaches the grove and power saws are available. The villagers refuse. Which statement describes the grove's trees correctly?
questions.a: Not a resource, since cutting fails the cultural condition. They are not a resource for the village, because the cultural condition fails. The road and saws make the trees technologically accessible and the price makes cutting economically feasible, but all three conditions must hold, and cutting trees in a sacred grove is culturally unacceptable.
o: Not a resource, since cutting fails the cultural condition
A resource, since two of the three conditions are met
Not a resource, since cutting them is not yet affordable
A resource, since the trees occur in Nature and have real value

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's idea of a resource.
1. Anything in our environment that humans did not create is already a resource, whether or not it can be used.
2. A tree is seen as a resource when its wood is cut and made into furniture.
3. Natural resources are materials and substances that occur in Nature and are valuable to humans.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false: that describes Nature; an element of Nature becomes a resource only when humans use it and it meets the chapter's conditions.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: Choose any three objects in your classroom. For each, name the element of Nature it can be traced back to. Then, for one of them, say what made that element a resource and which of the chapter's three conditions had to hold for it.
questions.a: Any consistent answer, for example: a wooden desk traces to a tree; a steel almirah to iron ore; a water bottle's contents to a river or well. For the desk: the tree became a resource when people cut it and made furniture from it; it had to be technologically accessible (tools to fell and saw it), economically feasible (worth the cost) and culturally acceptable (not from a sacred grove).
s: Three objects each traced to an element of Nature
What turned one element into a resource: human use
One element checked against the three conditions

questions.q: Write a situation, with a place and a resource, of something that was NOT a resource ten years ago but is one today. Name the condition that changed and say what changed it.
questions.a: Any consistent situation, for example: in 2015 a gas field 3,000 m below the seabed off the Andhra coast was beyond every rig, so it was not a resource; in 2025 a new rig reaches 3,500 m and the gas sells for more than it costs to extract. The condition that changed is technological accessibility (and, with it, the cost), brought about by the new rig.
s: A situation with a place, a resource and a 'then' and 'now'
Names the condition that changed
Says what caused the change, such as new technology or a change in cost

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A coal seam that machines can reach and that sells above its cost is certainly a resource, even if the community that owns the land objects to mining it.
Reason (R): For an entity to be called a resource it must be technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. R states the chapter's three conditions, all of which must hold; the community's objection means the cultural condition fails, so the seam is not yet a resource.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: 'A category is a shortcut that humans choose, not something written into Nature.' Justify this statement using the chapter's account of categorising natural resources.
questions.a: (1) We categorise by choosing some shared characteristics, or criteria; the choice is ours. (2) We name the categories so that one word or a short phrase stands for the whole set, which is a shortcut. (3) When the names and meanings are shared, people can discuss ideas without describing each item and communicate better, as with 'living' and 'non-living'. (4) The chapter offers more than one criterion: by use (life, materials, energy) and by whether a resource is renewable. (5) The same resource lands in different groups depending on the criterion and the use, as coal is listed under both materials and energy; if groups were written into Nature, this could not happen. So categories are chosen human shortcuts.
s: Criteria are chosen by us
Naming lets one word stand for a set
Shared names help communication, with the living/non-living example
More than one criterion exists: use, and renewable or not
The same resource can be in different groups, which supports the statement

questions.q:
A village in Uttarakhand recorded how it used the wood it took from nearby forests (illustrative figures).
| Year | Wood used | Share burnt as fuel | Share made into beams, doors and furniture |
| 2000 | 2,000 quintals | 75% | 25% |
| 2020 | 1,500 quintals | 30% | 70% |
(a) In 2000, how much wood was used as a resource for energy and how much as a resource for materials?
(b) Repeat (a) for 2020.
(c) The forest and the wood did not change. What does the shift between the groups show about how the chapter groups resources?
(d) Gas cylinders reach the village and the fuel share falls to 10% by 2030, with the same total as in 2020. Predict how much wood is then in each group.
questions.a: (a) Energy: 75% of 2,000 = 1,500 quintals; materials: 500 quintals. (b) Energy: 30% of 1,500 = 450 quintals; materials: 1,050 quintals. (c) The grouping is by the use a resource is put to, not by what it is, so the same wood moves between groups when its use changes. (d) Energy: 10% of 1,500 = 150 quintals; materials: 1,350 quintals.
s: Part (a): 1,500 quintals for energy, 500 for materials
Part (b): 450 quintals for energy, 1,050 for materials
Part (c): groups are by use, so one resource can change group when its use changes
Part (d): 150 quintals for energy, 1,350 for materials

questions.q: A Class 8 quiz asks for a list that could be placed entirely under 'resources for energy'. Which list should a student choose?
questions.a: Natural gas, sunlight, wind, flowing water: all four are sources the chapter names for energy. Marble and gold are used to make objects (materials), and wheat grain is food (essential for life), so each other list has one item that does not belong.
o: Natural gas, sunlight, wind, flowing water
Petroleum, marble, wind, coal
Sunlight, gold, natural gas, coal
Wind, petroleum, wheat grain, sunlight, natural gas

questions.q: A town in Telangana loses its electricity supply for a whole week. Using the chapter's description of resources for energy, explain how the loss would hit (i) buildings, (ii) transportation and (iii) production, and say how this shows why the chapter calls energy a cornerstone of modern living.
questions.a: (1) Buildings: homes, schools and hospitals lose lights, fans and machines that run on electricity. (2) Transportation: electric trains and vehicles stop, and the movement of people and goods slows. (3) Production: workshops and factories cannot run their production processes, so goods stop being made. Since buildings, transport and production all depend on energy at once, losing it stops ordinary modern life, which is what 'cornerstone' means.
s: Effect on buildings
Effect on transportation
Effect on production, linked to the meaning of cornerstone

questions.q: The chapter calls the use-based grouping only 'one of the ways' to categorise natural resources. What does that wording tell a student?
questions.a: Another criterion would sort them into other groups. A different criterion would sort the same resources into other groups. The chapter goes on to a second way, renewable or not. Categories depend on the criterion we choose, so the use-based scheme is neither the only correct one nor a mistake.
o: Another criterion would sort them into other groups
The use-based groups are not correct for India
Only resources for energy have a second grouping
Each resource can fit only one group in each scheme

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Gold made into a necklace is a resource for materials.
Reason (R): Resources for materials are used only to make useful objects, never things of beauty.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Gold shaped into a necklace is a physical object created from a natural resource, so it is a resource for materials. R is false: the chapter says we make objects for utility or to create things of beauty, as when wood is carved into a statuette.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the grouping in Column B.
Column A: 1. Marble cut into floor tiles for a school hall  2. Wind turning turbine blades on a Tamil Nadu ridge  3. Well water a family in Bihar drinks  4. Coal labelled 'cannot be replenished at the rate we use it'
Column B: a. a resource essential for life  b. a grouping by a criterion other than use  c. a resource for energy  d. a resource for materials
questions.a: 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b. Tiles are objects made from marble (materials); turbines turn wind into energy; drinking water is essential for life; 'cannot be replenished at the rate we use it' sorts coal by whether it is renewable, a different criterion from use.

questions.q: True or False? 'A single natural resource such as water can belong to more than one use-based group, depending on the use it is put to.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The grouping is by the use we put a resource to. Water drunk is essential for life, and the chapter also lists water among the sources of energy, as when flowing water is turned into electricity.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the groups are by use, and water is listed both as essential for life and as a source of energy

questions.q: Kiran says: 'If we sorted the same natural resources by whether they can be replaced, we would get groups different from the use-based ones, and neither way of sorting would be wrong.' Is she right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. A category depends on the criterion chosen: the chapter first groups resources by use (life, materials, energy) and then gives a second way, renewable or not. The two criteria cut the same resources differently; for example, coal and sunlight are both resources for energy, but coal is non-renewable while sunlight is renewable. Each grouping is useful for a different purpose, so neither is wrong.
s: Verdict: yes, she is right
Reason: categories depend on the chosen criterion; the chapter gives two
An example where the two criteria group resources differently

questions.q: Here is a category description: 'a resource for materials, used to create a thing of beauty rather than a thing of utility'. Write a situation from an Indian craft that fits it. Then explain why the resource in your situation belongs to the materials group and not the energy group.
questions.a: Any consistent situation, for example: a craftsman in Agra carves white marble into a small decorative inlaid box that is kept on a shelf for its beauty. Explanation: a physical object is created out of the marble, which is what the materials group covers, whether the object is for use or beauty; the marble is not being burnt or turned into electricity, so it is not a resource for energy.
s: A situation in which a natural material is shaped into an object of beauty
Reason it is materials: an object is created from it
Reason it is not energy: it is not used to obtain energy

questions.q:
A microhydel plant in Himachal Pradesh stands beside a fast hill stream.
(a) Which natural resource does the plant use, and into what does it convert it?
(b) Using (a), in which use-based group does that resource fall here, and why?
questions.a: (a) It uses the power of flowing water and converts it into electricity. (b) Resources for energy, because the water is being used here as a source of energy, not drunk or made into an object.
s: Part (a): flowing water converted into electricity
Part (b): resource for energy, because of the use it is put to here

questions.q:
A carpenter in Saharanpur cuts one log into two parts. From one he makes a study table; from the other he carves a wooden elephant to sell as a decoration.
(a) What different purpose does each object serve?
(b) Using (a), explain why both still place the wood in the same use-based group.
questions.a: (a) The table serves utility; the carved elephant is a thing of beauty that enriches life. (b) In both cases humans create a physical object out of the wood, and the chapter's group 'resources for materials' covers objects made for utility and for beauty, so the wood is a resource for materials either way.
s: Part (a): utility for the table, beauty for the elephant
Part (b): both are objects made from wood, so the wood is a resource for materials

questions.q:
The panchayat of a village near Raniganj, West Bengal, forms one committee for each use-based group of natural resources. The village depends on a well, paddy fields, a bamboo grove, a sand bed used for house-building and solar panels on the school roof. Last year it logged these complaints (illustrative): drinking water 40, grain shortage 5, bamboo supply 6, sand for houses 4, power cuts 9.
(a) Which of the five resources would sit with the committee for resources essential for life, and which with materials and with energy?
(b) How many complaints would each committee receive?
(c) What share of all complaints goes to the life committee?
(d) The panchayat can hire one extra clerk for one committee. Which committee should get the clerk, and what do the figures show?
questions.a: (a) Life: the well and the paddy fields; materials: the bamboo grove and the sand bed; energy: the solar panels (sunlight). (b) Life: 40 + 5 = 45; materials: 6 + 4 = 10; energy: 9. (c) 45 of 64 complaints, about 70 per cent. (d) The committee for resources essential for life: it receives 45 of the 64 complaints, far more than the materials committee (10) or the energy committee (9).
s: Part (a): well and paddy to life, bamboo and sand to materials, solar to energy
Part (b): 45, 10 and 9 complaints
Part (c): about 70 per cent (45 of 64)
Part (d): the life committee, with 45 of 64 complaints

questions.q: A bakery in Pune bakes bread in a coal-fired oven, makes its shelves from wood and kneads its dough with water from a borewell. Which row sorts the three by the use each is put to here?
questions.a: Coal for energy, wood for materials, water essential for life. Coal: for energy; wood: for materials; water: essential for life. The oven burns coal for heat, the shelves are objects made from wood, and the dough needs water that people cannot make. The other rows swap these uses.
o: Coal for energy, wood for materials, water essential for life
Coal for materials, wood for energy, water essential for life
Coal for energy, wood for life, water for materials
Coal for life, wood for materials, water for energy

questions.q:
A river valley in Himachal Pradesh supplies its people in many ways: villagers drink the river water, a microhydel plant turns the flowing water into electricity, carpenters make house beams from deodar trees, and farmers grow food on the valley's soil.
(a) Which of these uses fall in the group 'essential for life'?
(b) Which use falls in 'resources for materials'?
(c) Which use falls in 'resources for energy'?
(d) The school in the valley adds rooftop solar panels. In which use-based group does sunlight fall, and which two natural sources now supply the valley's energy?
(e) Analyse what the valley shows about using one criterion to describe a whole region's resources.
questions.a: (a) Drinking water and food from the soil. (b) Deodar wood made into house beams. (c) Flowing water turned into electricity by the microhydel plant. (d) Sunlight is a resource for energy; the valley's energy now comes from flowing water and sunlight. (e) One criterion gives a quick, shared way to talk about the valley's resources in three words, but it describes uses rather than things, so the same resource can be counted twice; a second criterion, such as renewable or not, would be needed to say how long those resources will last.
s: Part (a): drinking water and food from the soil
Part (b): deodar wood for beams
Part (c): flowing water for electricity
Part (d): sunlight is a resource for energy, and the valley's two energy sources are flowing water and sunlight
Part (e): one criterion is a useful shortcut but describes uses, and another criterion answers other questions

questions.q:
Read the statements about categorising natural resources.
1. A piece of wood carved into a statuette for its beauty is still a resource for materials.
2. The use-based criterion sorts natural resources by what they are made of.
3. Sunlight and wind are listed among the sources of energy, along with coal and petroleum.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: the use-based criterion sorts resources by the uses we put them to (life, materials, energy), not by what they are made of.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
2 only

questions.q: A builder in Bengaluru has a slab of granite cut and polished to make a kitchen counter. Under the chapter's use-based criterion, the granite here is a resource
questions.a: for materials, because humans are creating a physical object from it for their utility. It is not burnt or used to make electricity (energy), and it is not something life cannot exist without, like air, water or food.
o: for materials
for energy
essential for life
for both energy and life

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A hill village whose spring has dried up cannot simply make a new source of drinking water for itself.
Reason (R): We cannot make the air we breathe, the water we drink, or the soil which gives us food.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true and R explains A. Water is among the resources essential for life that humans cannot make, so the village has to find or restore a source rather than manufacture one.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What do we use when we categorise things, according to the chapter, and what do we do with the groups?
(b) Using (a), explain how a district officer gains by writing 'resources for energy' in a report instead of listing every item.
questions.a: (a) We use shared characteristics, called criteria, to form groups, and we name the categories so we can refer to them in one word or a short phrase. (b) The single name stands for the whole set (coal, water, petroleum, sunlight, wind and so on), so readers who share the meaning understand at once without each item being described, and the officer communicates more effectively.
s: Part (a): criteria (shared characteristics) and naming the groups
Part (b): one shared name stands for the set and saves describing each item

questions.q: A student writes: 'Gold, coal and wood belong only to the group resources for materials.' Find the error and correct the sentence using the chapter's three groups.
questions.a: Coal is wrong in the sentence: the chapter lists coal among resources for materials and also among sources of energy (with water, petroleum, natural gas, sunlight and wind). Corrected: gold and wood are resources for materials; coal is a resource for materials and also for energy.
s: The error: coal does not belong only to materials
The correction: coal is in both materials and energy; gold and wood are materials

questions.q: A thermal power station in Korba burns coal to produce electricity. Under the use-based criterion, the coal burnt there is a resource for ___.
questions.a: energy

questions.q:
A school in Pune keeps a compost pit. Vegetable peels and fallen leaves go in, and months later the compost feeds the school garden.
(a) Which feature of Nature's cycles is the pit copying?
(b) Using (a), the chapter says industrial wastes often cannot decay to become the food of some lifeform. What does that tell you about putting such waste into the pit?
questions.a: (a) Nature works in cycles where there is no waste: what is discarded, like a fallen tree, is fed on by bacteria, fungi and insects and becomes soil for new growth. (b) Such waste cannot be fed on, so it would not become compost or food for any lifeform; it would stay as waste and stop the pit from working as a cycle.
s: Part (a): the no-waste cycle, discarded matter becomes soil for new growth
Part (b): waste that cannot decay cannot be fed on, so it breaks the cycle in the pit

questions.q:
A school in Lucknow has 40 students in Class 8. The chapter gives these figures: a mature tree produces about 275 litres of oxygen a day, and a human being needs about 350 litres of oxygen a day.
(a) About how much oxygen do the 40 students need in one day?
(b) What is the least number of mature trees whose daily oxygen would cover that need?
(c) The class plants one tree per student. When the trees are mature, by how much will their daily oxygen fall short of the class's need?
(d) Why should all these answers be treated as estimates, according to the chapter?
(e) The chapter says a person's need changes with activity. If the students spend the day playing football and need more than 350 litres each, does the number of trees needed go up or down? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 40 x 350 = 14,000 litres. (b) 14,000 / 275 = 50.9, so at least 51 trees. (c) 40 trees give 40 x 275 = 11,000 litres, which is 14,000 - 11,000 = 3,000 litres short each day. (d) The chapter says a tree's oxygen output varies a little with the type of tree, and a person's need changes with activity, height and weight, so both figures are 'about'. (e) Up: each tree still gives about 275 litres, but the people need more than 350 litres each, so more trees are needed to cover the same students.
s: Part (a): 14,000 litres
Part (b): 51 trees, rounding 50.9 up
Part (c): 3,000 litres short
Part (d): figures vary with tree type and with a person's activity and body
Part (e): the number goes up, because need rises while a tree's output stays about the same

questions.q:
Two rivers in Tamil Nadu, the Veli and the Tara, flow past towns of similar size (illustrative account). Three years ago a factory on each river was discharging untreated waste that could not decay, and neither river had fish below its factory. Since then the Veli's factory has treated its waste, and fish have returned to the stretch below it. The Tara's factory has gone on discharging as before, and its stretch still has no fish. Above both factories fish thrive.
(a) Why do fish thrive above the factories?
(b) Why did both rivers lose their fish below the factories?
(c) What does the Veli show about Nature's ability once the cause is removed?
(d) Predict what will be found below the Tara's factory in three more years if nothing changes, and what would be found if the factory began treating its waste today.
questions.a: (a) Nothing breaks Nature's cycle there: what one living thing discards another consumes, with no waste, so the river supports life. (b) The waste could not decay to become the food of some lifeform, so it disturbed the cycle of restoration and regeneration and made the water unable to support life. (c) Once the cause was removed, Nature restored the stretch and life returned: restoration and regeneration working again. (d) If nothing changes, still no fish, because the cycle stays broken; if it began treating its waste, fish would be likely to return over time, as they did below the Veli's factory.
s: Part (a): the cycle is unbroken, so the river supports life
Part (b): waste that cannot decay breaks the cycle of restoration and regeneration
Part (c): with the cause removed, Nature restored the stretch
Part (d): no fish if nothing changes; fish likely to return if the waste is treated

questions.q:
(a) Describe one human action in an Indian town, other than discharging waste into water, that makes Nature lose her ability to restore and regenerate.
(b) Suggest one intervention that would help restore Nature's cycle in that case, and say how it helps.
questions.a: Any consistent pair, for example: (a) Clearing a hillside of its trees for housing. (b) Planting the tree types that originally grew there, which give food and shelter to birds, squirrels and other creatures so that life can return.
s: Part (a): a real human action that breaks a natural cycle, not waste discharge
Part (b): an intervention that removes or reduces that cause, with how it helps

questions.q: The chapter's opening quotation calls Nature 'the ultimate regenerator and recycler of all resources'. Evaluate this description, using what the chapter says about restoration, regeneration, the no-waste cycle and ecosystem functions, and also the limit the chapter shows.
questions.a: (1) Restoration: Nature heals, renews and maintains herself; a cut heals and a forest recovers after a wildfire. (2) Regeneration: she goes further and creates new life, as new trees grow from seeds in enriched soil. (3) Recycling: Nature works in cycles with no waste; a fallen tree is fed on by bacteria, fungi and insects and becomes soil. (4) She also performs functions such as filtering water, preventing soil erosion and producing oxygen, which become services when humans benefit. (5) Limit: the description holds only while her cycles are not broken; industrial wastes that cannot decay disturb the cycle and can make a river poisonous. So the description is fair for Nature left to her rhythm, but it is not a guarantee against human damage.
s: Restoration with an example
Regeneration with an example
The no-waste cycle of the fallen tree
Ecosystem functions and services
The limit: wastes that cannot decay break the cycle; balanced judgement

questions.q: Using the chapter's figures (a mature tree produces about 275 litres of oxygen a day; a person needs about 350 litres a day), show that one mature tree cannot meet even one person's daily need. Then find the least number of mature trees that would cover a family of five.
questions.a: One tree gives about 275 litres, which is 350 - 275 = 75 litres less than one person needs, so one tree cannot cover one person. A family of five needs 5 x 350 = 1,750 litres; 1,750 / 275 = 6.36, so at least 7 trees are needed (7 x 275 = 1,925 litres; 6 trees give only 1,650).
s: Shows the 75-litre shortfall for one person
Family need: 1,750 litres
At least 7 trees, rounding 6.36 up

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A tree that falls in a forest does not end up as waste.
Reason (R): A mature tree produces about 275 litres of oxygen per day.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but R does not explain A. The fallen tree is not waste because bacteria, fungi and insects feed on it and it enriches the soil for new growth; the oxygen a living tree produces has nothing to do with that.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'Because Nature works in cycles with no waste, every waste that humans produce, such as industrial effluent, will be fed on by some lifeform.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The no-waste cycle holds for what Nature itself discards, like a fallen tree. The chapter says industrial wastes frequently cannot decay to become the food of some lifeform, and then they disturb the cycle instead of joining it.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: industrial wastes often cannot decay into food for any lifeform and so break the cycle

questions.q: The chapter opens with a quotation calling for an economy that repurposes used resources, minimises waste and replenishes what is depleted. A town council in Maharashtra must pick one plan. Which plan fits that idea best?
questions.a: Reuse treated waste water and replant land cleared for housing. Reuse treated waste water and replant cleared land: it repurposes used resources, cuts waste and replenishes what has been lost. Each other plan does only part of it or does the opposite.
o: Reuse treated waste water and replant land cleared for housing
Recycle waste plastic, but burn more coal to run the recycling units
Plant fast-growing trees, but keep letting factory waste into the river
Replace old goods often, since factories then keep more people employed

questions.q: Sunita says: 'Nature always heals herself, so a river poisoned by factory waste will recover on its own, whatever we keep doing.' Is she right? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The chapter does say Nature heals, renews and maintains herself, as when a forest recovers after a wildfire. But it also says factory wastes discharged into rivers often cannot decay to become the food of some lifeform; this disturbs Nature's cycle of restoration and regeneration itself, so the river becomes poisonous and cannot support life. While the waste keeps coming, the healing process is the thing being broken, which is why the chapter asks what interventions can restore Nature's cycle.
s: Verdict: no
Waste that cannot decay disturbs the cycle of restoration and regeneration
So healing cannot be assumed while the cause continues; interventions are needed

questions.q:
Read the statements about Nature's cycles.
1. In Nature's cycles there is no waste, because what one process discards another consumes.
2. Industrial waste that cannot decay can disturb Nature's cycle so that a river becomes poisonous and cannot support life.
3. Restoration is the process of returning something to its original healthy state after it has been degraded or damaged.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three: 1, 2 and 3. All three are correct: each restates what the chapter says about Nature's no-waste cycles, about waste that cannot decay, and about restoration.
o: All three: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: A factory's waste cannot decay to become the food of any lifeform, so it disturbs Nature's cycle of restoration and ___.
questions.a: regeneration

questions.q: The chapter's opening quotation asks for an economy that repurposes used resources, minimises waste and replenishes depleted resources. For your school, give one action for each of these three aims and say how each copies something Nature does.
questions.a: Any consistent answers, for example: Repurposing: reuse the blank pages of old notebooks for rough work, as Nature's cycle reuses what one process discards. Minimising waste: compost canteen peels so that nothing is left over, as the no-waste forest cycle does. Replenishing: plant trees on bare ground, as Nature regenerates what was lost.
s: An action for repurposing, linked to a natural process
An action for minimising waste, linked to a natural process
An action for replenishing, linked to a natural process

questions.q: Four events are described. Which one shows regeneration going beyond restoration?
questions.a: New saplings sprouting in soil enriched by a fallen tree. New saplings sprouting from seeds in soil enriched by a fallen tree: regeneration is Nature creating new life. A healing cut and a forest recovering after a wildfire are the chapter's examples of restoration, a return to the original healthy state; cleaning a river to its old state is also a return, not new life.
o: New saplings sprouting in soil enriched by a fallen tree
A cut on a child's knee healing over in a week
A forest recovering its earlier cover a few years after a fire
A river cleaned so that it flows as clear as before

questions.q: A panchayat in Kerala wants to bring life back to a hillside that was cleared for housing years ago. Following the chapter, which choice of trees would best restore the ecosystem?
questions.a: The tree types that originally grew on that hillside. The types of trees that originally grew there: the chapter says planting them restores the ecosystem, as they give food and shelter to birds, squirrels and other creatures so life returns. Trees chosen only for timber, only for people's fruit, or simply for speed are not what the chapter describes.
o: The tree types that originally grew on that hillside
Whichever trees will give the most timber to sell
Only fruit trees whose produce the villagers themselves can eat
Any trees at all, so long as they grow fastest

questions.q:
A forest stands beside a village in Odisha (illustrative figures). Its roots hold the soil on the slope above the village fields, and its trees filter the water of the stream the village drinks from. A third of the forest was cleared some years ago; since then the panchayat has had to spend Rs 1.8 lakh a year on filtering the stream water. Assume that the yearly filtering cost rises in proportion to the share of the forest cleared. A timber firm now offers Rs 3 lakh a year for the remaining two-thirds.
(a) What ecosystem function does the filtering plant now replace?
(b) What ecosystem service did the village receive free before, and what turns the function into a service?
(c) What would the yearly filtering cost be if the whole forest were cleared, and by how much would it rise from today's?
(d) Should the panchayat accept the offer? Use (c) and name one other service the village would lose.
questions.a: (a) The forest's natural filtering of water, an ecosystem function. (b) Clean drinking water; it is a service because the villagers benefit from the function. (c) Cleared share 3 thirds: 3 x Rs 1.8 lakh = Rs 5.4 lakh a year, a rise of Rs 5.4 - 1.8 = Rs 3.6 lakh. (d) No. The extra filtering cost, Rs 3.6 lakh a year, is more than the Rs 3 lakh offered, before counting protected farmland: with the trees gone, nothing holds the slope's soil and the fields lose protection from erosion.
s: Part (a): filtering water, an ecosystem function
Part (b): clean water; a function becomes a service when humans benefit
Part (c): Rs 5.4 lakh a year, a rise of Rs 3.6 lakh
Part (d): refuse, since Rs 3.6 lakh exceeds Rs 3 lakh, and protected farmland would also be lost

questions.q: Bees from a forest beside a farm in Haryana pollinate the farmer's mustard crop, and his harvest is good. How does the chapter describe what the farmer receives?
questions.a: An ecosystem service from the forest. An ecosystem service: the forest's natural workings are benefiting a human. Pollination by forest creatures is the function; it is called a service when humans gain from it. It is not restoration or regeneration, which are about Nature healing and creating new life.
o: An ecosystem service from the forest
An ecosystem function with no human gain
Restoration of the forest after damage
Regeneration of the farmer's own soil

questions.q:
A village pond in Haryana was cleaned and all dumping into it was stopped in 2022. By 2025 its old water plants have come back and frogs have appeared that were never recorded there before.
(a) Which parts of this recovery are restoration and which are regeneration?
(b) Using (a), what would be missing if the pond had been cleaned but no new life had ever appeared?
questions.a: (a) Restoration: the pond returning to its original healthy state, with its old plants back. Regeneration: new life appearing, the frogs that were never there before. (b) Regeneration would be missing: the pond would be restored, but Nature's ability to create new life and the conditions for thriving would not have shown itself.
s: Part (a): old plants back is restoration, new frogs is regeneration
Part (b): regeneration, the creation of new life, would be missing

questions.q:
A wildfire burns a grassland in Kutch, and over the next two seasons it returns to its earlier healthy state.
(a) Is this restoration or regeneration, as the chapter uses the words?
(b) Using (a), what more would have to happen for the process to count as regeneration as well?
questions.a: (a) Restoration: the grassland is returned to its original healthy state after damage, as with the chapter's forest recovering after a wildfire. (b) New life would have to be created, with the conditions for thriving, such as new plants growing from seeds; regeneration goes beyond restoration.
s: Part (a): restoration, a return to the original healthy state
Part (b): the creation of new life and conditions for thriving

questions.q:
Match each event in Column A with the description in Column B.
Column A: 1. A scraped knee heals back to healthy skin  2. Saplings grow from seeds in soil enriched by a fallen tree  3. A factory discharges waste that cannot decay into a river  4. People plant the tree species that originally grew on a cleared hillside
Column B: a. a break in Nature's cycle of restoration and regeneration  b. restoration by Nature herself  c. a human action that helps an ecosystem recover  d. regeneration: new life is created
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c. Healing returns the skin to its healthy state (restoration); new saplings are new life (regeneration); waste that cannot decay disturbs the cycle; replanting original species restores the ecosystem by human effort.

questions.q:
(a) Name the two factors the chapter gives, among several, that have led to the rising temperatures we are experiencing.
(b) Using (a), explain the chain that links these factors to the water supply of people living on the plains.
questions.a: (a) Fossil fuel-driven industrialisation and the cutting down of forests for agriculture and other purposes. (b) Rising temperatures make glaciers in some Himalayan places melt faster than precipitation can replace them; the rivers fed by this 'water tower' are then at risk, which threatens water security for people on the plains who depend on them.
s: Part (a): fossil fuel-driven industrialisation and cutting forests
Part (b): glaciers melt faster than replaced, so river-fed water security on the plains is threatened

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with the description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Sunlight falling on rooftop panels in Jodhpur  2. Iron ore dug from a mine  3. Petroleum pumped from below the seabed  4. Timber cut faster than the forest can grow trees
Column B: a. a non-renewable mineral  b. a non-renewable fossil fuel  c. a renewable resource that keeps returning  d. a renewable resource being depleted
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d. Sunlight is renewable and returns each day; iron is a non-renewable mineral; petroleum is a fossil fuel and non-renewable; timber harvested faster than regrowth is a renewable resource whose condition has been broken, so the forest is being depleted.

questions.q: Fish are a living resource that breeds every year, yet the chapter reports that tuna is on the decline. Which explanation matches the chapter?
questions.a: Commercial fishing took tuna faster than it renewed. Commercial fishing took tuna faster than it could renew. The chapter says the commercialisation of fishing led to over-fishing and a rapid decline, and even the agreements on control of fishing have not stopped the decline. Tuna is not called non-renewable, and traditional restraint protected fish rather than harming them.
o: Commercial fishing took tuna faster than it renewed
Tuna is a non-renewable resource like petroleum
Traditional bans on fishing cut the tuna's food
The fishing agreements themselves are what killed off the tuna

questions.q:
Two villages in Madhya Pradesh each own a forest of 3,000 trees of the same kind (illustrative figures). Village Tola cuts 200 trees a year and its forest regrows 150 a year. Village Uma cuts 400 trees a year and its forest regrows 450 a year, because its soil is richer.
(a) Under the chapter's condition for renewability, whose timber is still a renewable resource?
(b) Uma cuts twice as many trees as Tola, yet Uma is the one in the clear. Explain this puzzle.
(c) If Tola goes on as now, how many trees will its forest hold after 10 years, and in how many years will it be empty?
(d) Uma's panchayat proposes to raise its yearly cutting to 480 trees. Predict what happens to its forest and why.
questions.a: (a) Uma's: it cuts less than its forest regrows (400 against 450). (b) What matters is not how many trees are cut but whether cutting is faster than regrowth: the forest renews itself only if its natural rhythm of regeneration is not disturbed. Tola cuts less, but still faster than its forest regrows. (c) Net loss 200 - 150 = 50 trees a year: 3,000 - 500 = 2,500 trees after 10 years; empty in 3,000 / 50 = 60 years. (d) At 480 against a regrowth of 450 the forest loses 30 trees a year, so it would slowly deplete and timber would stop being renewable.
s: Part (a): Uma's timber, since its cutting is below its regrowth
Part (b): what matters is cutting against regrowth, not the number cut
Part (c): 2,500 trees after 10 years, empty in 60 years
Part (d): a loss of 30 trees a year, so timber stops being renewable

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's iron ore reserves, though large, are a non-renewable resource.
Reason (R): Non-renewable resources are created over long periods and cannot be replenished at the rate at which we use them.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true and R explains A. Size of a reserve does not make a resource renewable; iron is a mineral that cannot be replaced as fast as it is mined, which is exactly what R says.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) Classify (i) copper in a mine and (ii) the energy of flowing water as renewable or non-renewable, with the chapter's reason for each.
(b) Using (a), if both were used at the same fast rate for many years, which would the chapter expect to run out, and why?
questions.a: (a) Copper is non-renewable: it is created over long periods and cannot be replenished at the rate we use it. The energy of flowing water is renewable: rivers keep being fed by rain and melting glaciers. (b) Copper would run out, because it is not replaced as fast as it is used, whereas flowing water keeps returning so long as its natural cycle is not disturbed.
s: Part (a): copper non-renewable, flowing water renewable, each with its reason
Part (b): copper runs out, because it is not replenished at the rate it is used

questions.q: A village in Rajasthan has abundant sunshine and a small copper mine. Thinking about its grandchildren, the panchayat asks which resource's use today leaves less of it for the future. What is the correct answer?
questions.a: The copper, a non-renewable metal. The copper, because it is a non-renewable metal that cannot be replenished at the rate it is used. Sunlight is a renewable resource that keeps returning; using it today does not reduce tomorrow's supply. Both are resources, so neither 'both equally' nor 'neither' is right.
o: The copper, a non-renewable metal
The sunshine, since it is used daily
Both of them, to the same extent
Neither, as both are found in Nature

questions.q: Compare timber and coal as resources, and analyse what 'responsible use' means for each. Cover: (a) which category each belongs to and why; (b) the condition under which timber stays available; (c) what the chapter estimates about India's coal; (d) why rising demand matters for coal; (e) what responsible use means for each, in one line each.
questions.a: (a) Timber is renewable, since forests renew themselves; coal is non-renewable, since it is created over long periods and cannot be replenished at the rate we use it. (b) Timber stays available only if the natural rhythm is not disturbed, that is, if it is harvested no faster than the forest grows trees. (c) India's coal reserves may last another 50 years. (d) Electricity demand is rising as population expands and development accelerates, which pushes coal use up and would make the reserve run out sooner. (e) Timber: take it in limited quantities so the forest regenerates. Coal: use it judiciously to stretch it until sustainable options become widely available.
s: Part (a): categories with reasons
Part (b): timber's condition
Part (c): about 50 years of coal
Part (d): rising demand shortens the time
Part (e): responsible use stated for each

questions.q:
A state's coal reserve is 1,500 million tonnes and it now uses 30 million tonnes a year (illustrative figures). Sustainable alternatives are expected to become widely available in 45 years.
(a) How long would the reserve last at the present rate?
(b) If yearly use grows to 37.5 million tonnes, how long would it last?
(c) The chapter asks us to use non-renewables so that they last until alternatives are found. Which of (a) and (b) meets that aim, and by how many years does the other miss it?
(d) Name one step the chapter suggests for keeping coal use steady while the demand for electricity grows.
(e) Why does the chapter call its own 50-year figure for India an estimate?
questions.a: (a) 1,500 / 30 = 50 years. (b) 1,500 / 37.5 = 40 years. (c) The present rate meets the aim: 50 years lasts 5 years beyond the 45 needed; the higher rate runs out 45 - 40 = 5 years too early. (d) Make the switch to renewable sources of energy for as many purposes as possible. (e) Demand keeps changing as the population expands and development accelerates, so how long coal lasts depends on how fast it is used.
s: Part (a): 50 years
Part (b): 40 years
Part (c): the present rate meets the aim, with 5 years to spare; the higher rate falls 5 years short
Part (d): switch to renewable energy for as many purposes as possible
Part (e): demand changes, so the figure is an estimate

questions.q: Write a situation, with numbers, about a forest in an Indian state that leads to this conclusion: 'At this rate, the forest will be gone in 25 years.' Then show the working and name the condition for renewability that is being broken.
questions.a: Any consistent situation, for example: a forest in Madhya Pradesh has 15,000 trees and regrows 400 trees a year, but 1,000 trees are cut each year. Working: it loses 1,000 - 400 = 600 trees a year, and 15,000 / 600 = 25 years. Condition broken: timber is harvested faster than the forest can grow trees, so the natural rhythm of regeneration is disturbed.
s: A situation with stock, regrowth and harvest figures
Working that reaches 25 years
Names the broken condition: harvest faster than regrowth

questions.q: True or False? 'A village that plants a forest and each year harvests only as much timber as the forest regrows can keep taking timber from it for a long time.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Timber is renewable on one condition: the natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration must not be disturbed. Harvesting no faster than the forest grows trees keeps that rhythm, so timber can be taken in limited quantities for a long time.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: harvest within regrowth keeps the condition for renewability

questions.q: Farmers on the plains of Bihar depend on a river fed by Himalayan glaciers. Which warning from the chapter concerns them most directly?
questions.a: Glaciers are melting faster than precipitation replaces them. Glaciers in some places are melting faster than precipitation can replace them, which affects water security for people on the plains who depend on the 'water tower'. The chapter does not say river water is non-renewable, that glaciers are growing, or that rain alone feeds such rivers.
o: Glaciers are melting faster than precipitation replaces them
River water is a non-renewable resource like coal
Glaciers are growing because temperatures are rising
Their river is fed by rainfall alone, and not by any glaciers at all

questions.q:
Read the statements about renewable and non-renewable resources.
1. Timber is non-renewable, because a tree that is cut down is destroyed.
2. Non-renewable resources are those that never form in Nature at all.
3. Traditionally, some communities stopped fishing during the spawning season so that the fish population could be maintained.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. Only 3 is correct. Statement 1 is false: timber from forests is renewable if the forest is allowed to regenerate. Statement 2 is false: non-renewables are created over long periods; the problem is that they cannot be replenished at the rate we use them.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
All three: 1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A village woodlot regrows 600 quintals of firewood a year, and the villagers collect exactly 600 quintals every year. After ten years, the woodlot's stock has changed by ___ quintals.

The chapter says India's coal reserves may last another 50 years, and that electricity demand is rising.
(a) Which two developments does the chapter give as pushing demand up?
(b) Using (a), what would a rise in demand do to the 50-year estimate, and what does the chapter say we should do with coal until sustainable options are widely available?
questions.a: (a) The population is expanding and development work is accelerating. (b) Higher demand means coal is used faster, so the reserve would last fewer than 50 years. Until more sustainable options become widely available, the chapter says we must use the coal we have judiciously.
s: Part (a): expanding population and accelerating development work
Part (b): the estimate would shorten; use coal judiciously until alternatives are widely available

questions.q: Rohit says: 'Sunlight and timber are both renewable resources, so we can use both of them as much as we like.' Is he right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the chapter lists both solar energy and timber from forests as renewable resources. He is wrong that 'renewable' means unlimited use: the chapter says renewables stay renewable only on condition that the natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration is not disturbed. If timber is harvested faster than the forest can grow trees, the forest is eventually depleted.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: both are renewable in the chapter
Wrong part: the condition; harvesting timber faster than regrowth depletes the forest

questions.q: Kabir argues: 'New oil fields are discovered every few years, so petroleum is a renewable resource.' What is the flaw in his argument?
questions.a: Discovering more fields is not replenishing petroleum at the rate it is used. Finding new fields adds to what we know about, but petroleum, like other non-renewables, is not replenished as fast as we use it. Discovery is not replenishment.
o: Discovering more fields is not replenishing petroleum at the rate it is used
Oil fields count as renewable only when they lie below the sea
A resource is renewable if its known reserves are large enough
Renewable resources are the ones used to produce energy

questions.q:
A fishing cooperative manages a village lake in Odisha (illustrative figures). The lake holds about 20,000 fish and breeding adds about 3,000 fish a year; assume this stays constant. The members catch 2,500 fish a year at Rs 60 each. A trader offers Rs 50 each for 5,000 fish a year, taken every year until the lake is empty.
(a) What is the largest yearly catch that keeps the lake a renewable resource?
(b) Under the trader's plan, how many years until the lake is empty, and what would the cooperative earn in all?
(c) Under a catch of exactly the amount in (a), what would the cooperative earn at Rs 60 a fish over 20 years?
(d) The members want the lake to feed their children's generation, a 20-year horizon. Which plan should they choose, and by how much does it come out ahead?
questions.a: (a) 3,000 fish a year, the number breeding replaces. (b) The stock falls by 5,000 - 3,000 = 2,000 a year, so the lake is empty in 20,000 / 2,000 = 10 years; earnings 10 x 5,000 x Rs 50 = Rs 25 lakh. (c) 3,000 x Rs 60 = Rs 1.8 lakh a year; over 20 years, Rs 36 lakh. (d) The catch of 3,000 a year: Rs 36 lakh against Rs 25 lakh, Rs 11 lakh ahead, and the lake is still there after 20 years because the catch does not disturb the natural rhythm of regeneration.
s: Part (a): 3,000 fish a year
Part (b): 10 years and Rs 25 lakh
Part (c): Rs 36 lakh over 20 years
Part (d): the 3,000 catch, Rs 11 lakh ahead, and the lake survives

questions.q:
(a) Name one non-renewable resource your household uses every day, directly or indirectly, and say how it is used.
(b) Suggest a renewable substitute for that use, and one step your family could take to make the switch.
questions.a: Any consistent answer, for example: (a) Petroleum, as petrol in the scooter used for the school run. (b) A renewable substitute is electricity from sunlight; the family could charge an electric scooter from rooftop solar panels, or walk or cycle for short trips.
s: Part (a): a correct non-renewable resource and its daily use
Part (b): a matching renewable substitute and a realistic step

questions.q: A lake community has for generations stopped fishing during the fish spawning season. A trading firm now offers good prices and wants the community to fish all year. (a) Predict what happens to the lake's fish if the community accepts. (b) Which condition for a renewable resource is then broken? (c) Why does the chapter say the decline of a fish like tuna matters beyond the fish itself?
questions.a: (a) The fish population would be likely to fall, because the fish no longer get the chance to breed. (b) The natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration is disturbed, since fish are taken faster than they are replaced. (c) Tuna keeps the ocean ecosystem in balance by consuming smaller fish, shrimps and so on, so its decline upsets that balance.
s: Part (a): the fish population is likely to fall without a spawning season
Part (b): the rhythm of restoration and regeneration is disturbed
Part (c): tuna balances the ocean ecosystem by eating smaller fish and shrimps

questions.q: True or False? 'India has avoided the natural resource curse because it has very few natural resources.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says India has significant resources, for example coal, and has generally avoided the curse by investing in the development of industries that convert resources into products of higher value.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: India avoided the curse by investing in industries, not by having few resources

questions.q: Show that the amount of natural resources a country has cannot, on its own, tell us how prosperous it will be. Use the chapter's reasoning and a pair of illustrative countries.
questions.a: Take two illustrative countries with the same large reserves of ore. Country A sells only raw ore; Country B builds industries that turn ore into higher-value products. The chapter says resource-rich regions can grow more slowly when they cannot develop such industries (the paradox of plenty), while India avoided the curse by investing in them. Since the two countries have equal resources but different outcomes, the amount of resources alone cannot decide prosperity; what is done with them, through knowledge, governance and planning, does.
s: Sets up two countries with equal resources and different choices
Uses the paradox of plenty and India's example
Concludes that resources alone cannot decide prosperity

questions.q:
A steel plant is set up near iron-ore mines in a hilly district.
(a) Give one benefit the plant brings to local people and one to others in the area.
(b) Give one cost it may bring that could lead to conflict, and say why.
questions.a: (a) Local people: jobs at the plant. Others: a township grows around it and expands economic opportunities, with more modern facilities that improve the quality of life. (b) Displacement: people living in the resource-rich area may be moved from their homes, or their sacred places may be threatened, which the chapter says leads to conflicts.
s: Part (a): a benefit for local people and one for others
Part (b): displacement or threatened sacred places, leading to conflict

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sharing the water of the Kaveri among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry needed negotiations and deft management.
Reason (R): Nature does not pay attention to political boundaries.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true and R explains A. The river flows through several states, so its water cannot be divided by state borders and has to be shared by agreement.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: 'Where natural resources happen to lie shapes far more than the economy.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Cover settlements, trade, relations between states or countries, conflict, and the costs that come with industry near resources.
questions.a: (1) Natural resources are not evenly distributed across the planet or even within countries, and this shapes human settlements: industries near resources create jobs, and townships grow around them with more modern facilities. (2) Trade: national and international trade depend on the geographical location of resources; with human knowledge and skills they give unique products such as Wootz steel, and trade fuelled large empires in India. (3) Relations: Nature does not pay attention to political boundaries, so resources like river water must be shared by negotiation, as the Kaveri is among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry. (4) Conflict: many wars have been fought, and still are, to gain control over natural resources. (5) Costs: people in resource-rich areas have been displaced, and sacred places threatened, leading to conflicts. So location shapes where people live, what they trade, how they deal with neighbours and what they fight over.
s: Settlements and townships near resources
Trade and Wootz steel, empires
Sharing across boundaries, the Kaveri
Wars over control of resources
Costs: displacement and threatened sacred places

questions.q: Interpret why the geographical location of natural resources matters for trade. Use Wootz steel and the chapter's remark about empires in your answer.
questions.a: (1) Because resources are unevenly spread, national and international trade depend on where they are found: places that lack a resource must get it from places that have it. (2) A resource on its own is not enough; combined with human knowledge and skills it can become a unique product, like Wootz steel, which others want. (3) Such trade brought wealth, and the chapter notes that trade fuelled the development of large empires in India, so location, through trade, shaped history.
s: Uneven location makes trade necessary
Resources plus skill give unique products such as Wootz steel
Trade fuelled large empires in India

questions.q: A region (illustrative; not a real place) has a metal resource, and its people have combined it with their own knowledge and skills to make a product that people in other regions want to buy. Which idea from the chapter does this illustrate?
questions.a: Resources joined with human knowledge and skills create unique products that trade. Trade depends on where resources lie, and resources combined with knowledge and skills can create unique products, as with the chapter's example of Wootz steel.
o: Resources joined with human knowledge and skills create unique products that trade
Abundant resources do not guarantee prosperity, the paradox of plenty
Industries near resources displace local people from their homes
Nature pays no attention to political boundaries, so water is shared

questions.q: A state earns most of its income by selling raw ore that will be mined out in 25 years, and it has built no industry that uses the ore. Which phrase from the chapter describes such income best?
questions.a: A temporary windfall rather than a lasting benefit. The chapter says knowledge, good governance and planning decide whether resources become lasting benefits or temporary windfalls.
o: A temporary windfall rather than a lasting benefit
A lasting benefit, because the ore is a valuable resource
An ecosystem service received from Nature
Proof that the state has avoided the resource curse

questions.q:
A company's brochure for a proposed coal mine in a forested district (illustrative figures) says: 'The mine will employ 1,200 local people, and a township will grow around it with schools and a hospital for all. A few families will have to move.' District records show that the mine would displace 300 families of about 5 members each, from villages beside a hill they hold sacred.
(a) Which two benefits in the brochure match benefits the chapter names for industries near resources?
(b) How many people would be displaced, and how does that compare with the 1,200 jobs?
(c) Besides displacement, which cost named by the chapter does the brochure leave out?
(d) Judge the brochure as a source: is its picture of the project complete? Use (a)-(c) and the chapter's remark about benefits and costs.
questions.a: (a) Employment for local people, and a township with more modern facilities that improve quality of life. (b) 300 x 5 = 1,500 people displaced, more than the 1,200 jobs. (c) The threat to sacred places, which the chapter says leads to conflicts. (d) Not complete. The chapter says such benefits are often accompanied by costs in the short and long term; the brochure lists the benefits but calls the displacement of 1,500 people 'a few families' and omits the threat to the sacred hill, so it cannot be relied on as the whole picture.
s: Part (a): jobs for local people and township with modern facilities
Part (b): 1,500 displaced, more than the 1,200 jobs
Part (c): the threat to sacred places
Part (d): incomplete; benefits come with costs the brochure understates or omits

questions.q:
A small island nation (illustrative) has a busy port but no coal, oil or iron ore.
(a) Which two effects of the uneven distribution of resources does this most affect?
(b) Using (a), why might its dealings with resource-rich countries matter more to it than to a country with plenty?
questions.a: (a) Trade patterns and international relations. (b) What it lacks it must obtain through trade, so its supply depends on agreements with countries that have those resources; the chapter says the uneven spread shapes both trade and relations between countries.
s: Part (a): trade patterns and international relations
Part (b): it must trade for what it lacks, so those relations matter more

questions.q:
Match each example in Column A with the idea in Column B that it shows.
Column A: 1. Kaveri water shared by Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry  2. Families moved out of their villages to open a mine  3. A resource-rich country whose economy grows slowly  4. Wootz steel
Column B: a. resources combined with knowledge and skills  b. a cost of industry near resources  c. the paradox of plenty  d. Nature pays no attention to political boundaries
questions.a: 1-d, 2-b, 3-c, 4-a. The Kaveri crosses state boundaries; displacement is a cost of industry near resources; slow growth despite plenty is the paradox; Wootz steel came from resources joined to human skill.

questions.q:
A river rises in State A and then flows through State B (illustrative figures). In a dry year it carries 100 units of water. State A wants 70 units and State B wants 60. A proposal shares the water in proportion to the two wants.
(a) By how much do the two wants exceed the water available?
(b) How many units would each state get under the proportional share, to one decimal place?
(c) Which idea from the chapter explains why neither state alone can settle the matter?
(d) In a wet year the river carries 150 units and the wants stay the same. Predict what happens to the tension and whether the sharing agreement still matters, and why.
questions.a: (a) 70 + 60 = 130 wanted against 100: 30 units too many. (b) State A: 70/130 x 100 = 53.8 units; State B: 60/130 x 100 = 46.2 units. (c) Nature does not pay attention to political boundaries: the river flows through both states, so its water is shared and sharing causes tension. (d) Both wants (130) are met from 150 units, so the tension eases; the agreement still matters, because in dry years the water is short again and, as with the Kaveri, negotiation and management keep peace and fair sharing.
s: Part (a): 30 units short
Part (b): 53.8 and 46.2 units
Part (c): Nature ignores political boundaries, so the river must be shared
Part (d): tension eases in a wet year, but the agreement still matters for dry years

questions.q: A state's iron ore lies in just two of its districts. A steel plant opens there and a township grows around it. Which outcome fits the chapter's account?
questions.a: Local jobs and facilities grow, along with costs such as displacement. Jobs and facilities grow for local people, along with costs such as displacement. The chapter says industries near resources create employment and townships, but the benefits are often accompanied by costs.
o: Local jobs and facilities grow, along with costs such as displacement
Every district of the state gains equally, since resources are spread evenly within a country
Only workers at the plant benefit, and no township grows around it
The two districts become prosperous for certain, whatever industries are built
