questions.q: Aman says: 'Two neighbouring states can quarrel over a river even if each of them has plenty of other resources, because the river does not stop at their border.' Is he right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter says Nature does not pay attention to political boundaries, which leads to tensions over sharing natural resources across states and countries. Being rich in other resources does not settle who gets a shared river's water; the Kaveri, shared among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, needed negotiations and deft management to keep peace.
s: Verdict: yes, he is right
Reason: Nature ignores political boundaries, so shared resources cause tension
Support: the Kaveri needed negotiation and management

questions.q: State P has large coal reserves and State Q has none, so Q's power plants buy their coal from P. Which statement from the chapter does this show?
questions.a: National trade depends on where natural resources are located. National trade depends on the geographical location of natural resources: Q buys from P because the coal lies in P. Resources are not evenly distributed, even within a country.
o: National trade depends on where natural resources are located
Resources are spread so evenly that states seldom need to trade
Nature draws its boundaries to match those of the states
A state with coal reserves is certain to be richer than one without

questions.q:
The chapter says that knowledge, good governance and strategic planning decide whether natural resources become lasting benefits or temporary windfalls.
(a) What is a 'temporary windfall' for a district that finds a rich ore?
(b) Using (a), name one thing from the chapter that such a district should invest in to make the benefit last.
questions.a: (a) Income that comes for a while, as long as the ore is dug and sold, and then stops, leaving little behind. (b) Industries that convert the ore into products of higher value, together with technology and skills.
s: Part (a): income that lasts only while the ore lasts
Part (b): higher-value industries with technology and skills

questions.q: The chapter says that human knowledge, good governance and strategic planning determine whether natural resources become lasting benefits or temporary windfalls. Analyse this claim with the help of the paradox of plenty and India's own path.
questions.a: (1) Abundant resources do not guarantee prosperity; regions rich in them can grow slowly, which economists call the natural resource curse or paradox of plenty. (2) The usual reason is that an economy cannot develop industries that convert its resources into products of higher value. (3) India has generally avoided the curse by investing in such industries to meet its growing needs, and the chapter's summary adds that the curse can be overcome by investing in technology and skills. (4) Even so, the challenge of balancing extraction with sustainability remains, so success is not automatic. (5) Hence the same resource can be a lasting benefit when knowledge, governance and planning turn it into industry and use it sustainably, or a temporary windfall when it is only extracted and sold; the claim is supported.
s: The paradox of plenty explained
Reason: no industries converting resources to higher value
India's path: investment in industries, technology and skills
The remaining challenge of sustainability
Judgement linking knowledge, governance and planning to lasting benefit

questions.q:
Read the statements about the distribution of natural resources.
1. Natural resources are unevenly spread across the planet but evenly spread within a single country.
2. Wootz steel shows how natural resources combined with human knowledge and skills can create unique products.
3. Industries located near natural resources bring benefits to local people and no costs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only. Only 2 is correct. Statement 1 is false: resources are not evenly distributed even within countries. Statement 3 is false: the benefits are often accompanied by costs, such as displacement and threats to sacred places.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Region P is rich in iron ore but sells almost all of it as raw ore, and its economy grows slowly. Region Q has little ore but has built industries that turn ore into machines, and it grows fast (illustrative). Which idea from the chapter explains Region P?
questions.a: The paradox of plenty: abundant resources do not guarantee prosperity, often because an economy cannot develop industries that convert resources into products of higher value, which is what P lacks. P is not short of resources, and nothing in the account is about cultural acceptability or Nature's no-waste cycle.
o: The paradox of plenty
The spread of resources being too uneven for P
Its ore failing the cultural-acceptability test
A break in Nature's cycle of restoration and regeneration

questions.q:
Country X sells all its bauxite raw. Country Y turns its bauxite into aluminium goods at home. Both have equally large reserves.
(a) Which country is more at risk of the paradox of plenty, according to the chapter?
(b) Using (a), what does the chapter say the at-risk country must develop to avoid the curse?
questions.a: (a) Country X: abundant resources do not guarantee prosperity, and an economy that cannot convert resources into products of higher value is the one that risks slower growth. (b) Industries that convert its resources into products of higher value, supported by investment in technology and skills.
s: Part (a): Country X, which sells raw bauxite
Part (b): industries converting resources into higher-value products, with technology and skills

questions.q:
Match each item from the Punjab story in Column A with what the chapter says about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. High-yielding varieties of wheat and paddy  2. Free power  3. Chemical pesticides and fertilisers  4. Rejuvenating ponds and tanks
Column B: a. a strategy for raising groundwater levels  b. needed more water than the traditional seeds  c. led to over-pumping of groundwater  d. dissolved in groundwater, causing health hazards
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-a. The new varieties needed more water; free power led to over-pumping; the chemicals dissolved in groundwater and caused health hazards; rejuvenating ponds and tanks is one of the strategies to raise groundwater levels.

questions.q: The chapter says Punjab fed a large proportion of our population and made India self-sufficient in food, yet almost 80 per cent of its area is now over-exploited. Explain in three points how both statements can be true.
questions.a: (1) The shift to high-yielding wheat and paddy in the 1960s, with free power and chemical inputs, gave large harvests, so food security was ensured for the short term. (2) This was done by drawing groundwater far faster than it could be restored and by using chemicals that dissolved in the water, so Nature was exploited beyond regeneration, at least in the short term. (3) The long-term consequences will take time and effort to heal, so short-term success and long-term damage can sit side by side.
s: Short-term food security from the shift to high-yielding crops
Water drawn beyond restoration, with chemicals in the groundwater
Long-term consequences need time and effort to heal

questions.q: Suppose almost 80 per cent of a 1,500 sq km district is classed as over-exploited for groundwater, as in Punjab. About ___ sq km of the district are then over-exploited.

In a farming block (illustrative figures), the water table was 5 m below ground in 1990 and has fallen by 0.6 m every year since.
(a) How deep was the water table after 20 years?
(b) At the same rate, about how many years after 1990 would it reach 30 m, the depth the chapter mentions for a large part of Punjab?
(c) After 20 years, the block adopts water harvesting and pond rejuvenation, and the fall slows to 0.2 m a year. From then, how many more years until it reaches 30 m?
(d) The chapter says that in much of Punjab the groundwater has become inaccessible down to about 30 metres. What does a water table that has fallen to that depth mean for a farmer's pump and costs?
(e) Is the block in (c) using its groundwater sustainably? Judge using the chapter's idea of over-exploitation.
questions.a: (a) 5 + 0.6 x 20 = 17 m. (b) (30 - 5) / 0.6 = 41.7, so about 42 years. (c) (30 - 17) / 0.2 = 65 more years. (d) Water above that depth is gone, so wells must go deeper, extraction costs rise, and the water may eventually be unavailable. (e) Not yet. The slower fall buys time, but the water table is still falling, so water is still drawn faster than it is restored; it is sustainable only when extraction no longer exceeds replenishment.
s: Part (a): 17 m
Part (b): about 42 years
Part (c): 65 more years
Part (d): deeper wells, rising cost, possible unavailability
Part (e): not yet sustainable while the table still falls

questions.q: After years of heavy use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, a farmer's fields in Uttar Pradesh give poorer crops each season. Which practices does the chapter say we should learn from to rebuild such soil?
questions.a: Cow dung and natural fertilisers, mulching and multi-cropping, the traditional practices that enabled holistic soil management. More chemicals or free power caused the problem in the first place, and growing only high-yielding varieties is part of the Punjab story, not the remedy.
o: Cow dung and natural fertilisers, mulching and multi-cropping
A different brand of chemical fertiliser in smaller doses, with more irrigation
Heavier pesticide sprays to protect the weak crop, with the same fertiliser
Shifting wholly to high-yielding wheat and paddy to raise the yield

questions.q: A farmer in Haryana has had to deepen his borewell twice in ten years, and his electricity and pumping costs have kept rising. In the chapter's chain of events, what is the stage that comes next if extraction goes on faster than the water table is replenished?
questions.a: The groundwater eventually becomes unavailable. The chapter's chain is: extraction faster than replenishment, a deficit that builds up, a higher cost of extraction, and finally unavailability. The farmer is already at the rising-cost stage. Deeper wells do not refill the water table, and nothing in the chain makes it rise again by itself.
o: The groundwater eventually becomes unavailable
The water table refills because wells are deeper
Pumping costs fall as the water gets used up
The aquifer becomes a non-renewable mineral

questions.q:
Two villages in one district get the same rain and have similar soil (illustrative figures). A farm in Village Abhay grows paddy and wheat with free power and heavy chemical use; its income is Rs 1,20,000 in year 1 and falls by Rs 4,000 each year as the water table sinks (now 32 m below ground) and pumping costs rise. A farm in Village Bhavna has rejuvenated tanks, harvests rain, uses cow dung and grows mixed crops; its income is Rs 80,000 a year for 3 years and then a steady Rs 1,00,000 a year (water table 9 m).
(a) Which village's practices match the Punjab caselet, and on which three points?
(b) What is each farm's total income over the first 5 years?
(c) In which year does Bhavna's running total first pass Abhay's, and what are the two totals after 20 years?
(d) The district's stated aim is a farm economy that still works 20 years from now. Which model should it promote, and what in the chapter supports the choice?
questions.a: (a) Abhay: water-hungry paddy and wheat, free power leading to over-pumping, and heavy chemical use. (b) Abhay: 5 x 1,20,000 - 4,000 x (0+1+2+3+4) = Rs 5,60,000; Bhavna: 3 x 80,000 + 2 x 1,00,000 = Rs 4,40,000. (c) Year 14 (Rs 13,16,000 against Rs 13,40,000); after 20 years Abhay Rs 16,40,000 and Bhavna Rs 19,40,000. (d) Bhavna's model. Abhay's farm pays more at first but falls behind from year 14, while its water table keeps sinking; the chapter says renewables should be used so that they can restore and regenerate, and that food security won in the short term leaves long-term consequences that take time and effort to heal.
s: Part (a): Abhay matches, on crops, free power and chemicals
Part (c): year 14; Rs 16,40,000 and Rs 19,40,000 after 20 years
Part (d): Bhavna's model, since it lasts and lets groundwater restore

questions.q: A growing city in Karnataka is running short of groundwater. Which of these is NOT one of the strategies the chapter lists for raising groundwater levels?
questions.a: Drilling deeper borewells to reach falling water. Drilling deeper borewells. It reaches water that is lower down but does nothing to refill the water table, and the chapter's chain shows it leads to higher costs and eventual unavailability. Water harvesting, rejuvenating ponds and tanks, cutting wasteful use, and processing and reusing water are the strategies the chapter names.
o: Drilling deeper borewells to reach falling water
Rejuvenating the city's old ponds, lakes and water tanks
Processing used water and reusing it
Traditional harvesting of rainwater

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Over-pumping of groundwater by farmers is still prevalent in much of India today.
Reason (R): The Green Revolution helped India become self-sufficient in food.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but R does not explain A. The chapter links the over-pumping that is still prevalent today to the supply of free power; India's self-sufficiency in food is a true but separate outcome of the Green Revolution.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) Name the three results that scientists warn the irresponsible treatment of natural resources has led to.
(b) In a village (illustrative), several kinds of birds, bees and butterflies that were common twenty years ago are no longer seen. Which of the three results in (a) does this show? Explain the term.
questions.a: (a) Pollution, biodiversity loss and climate change, taking place at an increased pace in recent years. (b) Biodiversity loss: the decline in the variety of life on Earth; the village now has fewer kinds of living things than before.
s: Part (a): pollution, biodiversity loss and climate change
Part (b): biodiversity loss, the decline in the variety of life

questions.q: Four blocks in a district are measured for groundwater each year (illustrative units drawn and units Nature restores): Block 1: 90 drawn, 85 restored. Block 2: 90 drawn, 40 restored. Block 3: 40 drawn, 90 restored. Block 4: 60 drawn, 60 restored. Which block fits the chapter's meaning of 'over-exploited'?
questions.a: Block 2, drawing 90 where only 40 are restored. Block 2: it draws water at a rate much greater than the rate at which restoration is possible. Block 1 draws only slightly more than is restored, and Blocks 3 and 4 draw no more than is restored.
o: Block 2, drawing 90 where only 40 are restored
Block 1, drawing 90 where 85 are restored
Block 3, drawing 40 where 90 are restored
Block 4, drawing 60 where 60 are restored

questions.q:
In a village (illustrative), the ground is recharged with 8 units of water a year while farmers draw 12 units.
(a) What is the yearly deficit, and how large will it have grown after 10 years if nothing changes?
(b) Using (a), explain why the farmers' cost of getting water will rise.
questions.a: (a) 12 - 8 = 4 units a year; after 10 years, 4 x 10 = 40 units. (b) As the deficit builds up the water table falls, so water has to be pumped from deeper down; the chapter says this leads to a higher cost of extraction and eventually to the water being unavailable.
s: Part (a): 4 units a year, 40 units after 10 years
Part (b): a falling water table means deeper pumping and higher cost

questions.q: True or False? 'Even if Punjab's farmers had used no chemical pesticides or fertilisers, the shift to high-yielding wheat and paddy in the 1960s would still have raised their use of groundwater.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the high-yielding varieties required more water than the traditional seeds, and farmers began to extract groundwater to meet this need; the chemicals were a separate effect that dissolved in the water.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the new varieties needed more water, so farmers pumped more, regardless of chemicals

questions.q: Explain what 'stewardship' of natural resources means in this chapter, using one renewable and one non-renewable resource as examples.
questions.a: Stewardship means respecting Nature and using resources responsibly: renewables in a way that lets them restore and regenerate, and non-renewables judiciously. Example: groundwater (renewable) should not be pumped faster than the water table is replenished; coal (non-renewable) should be used carefully so that it lasts until sustainable options are available.
s: Meaning: restoration and regeneration of renewables, judicious use of non-renewables
One correct example of each kind

questions.q: Harpreet says: 'Punjab's groundwater crisis had a single cause: farmers wasting water.' Is she right? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The chapter shows several factors combining. (1) In the 1960s farmers shifted to high-yielding wheat and paddy that needed more water than traditional seeds, so they began to extract groundwater. (2) The supply of free power led to over-pumping. (3) Modern farming also required chemical pesticides and fertilisers, which dissolved in the groundwater. The result was water inaccessible to about 30 metres and unsafe, so a single cause of 'wasting water' does not match the chapter.
s: Verdict: no
High-yielding varieties needing more water, and free power leading to over-pumping
Chemicals dissolving in groundwater: the combined effect, not one cause

questions.q:
(a) How did the supply of free power affect the use of groundwater in Punjab?
(b) Using (a), if electricity for pumping were charged by use, which of the three Punjab factors (high-yielding varieties, free power, chemical use) would be weakened, and which two would remain?
questions.a: (a) With power free, pumping cost the farmer little, so groundwater was over-pumped. (b) The free-power factor would be weakened, since pumping would cost the farmer something. The need of high-yielding varieties for more water, and the use of chemical pesticides and fertilisers, would remain.
s: Part (a): free power led to over-pumping
Part (b): free power weakened; high-yielding varieties' water need and chemical use remain

questions.q:
Read the statements about stewardship and groundwater.
1. Stewardship means using natural resources so that renewables can restore and regenerate and non-renewables are used responsibly and judiciously.
2. In most states, the water table is replenished faster than farmers extract groundwater.
3. The traditional seeds grown in Punjab before the 1960s needed more water than the high-yielding varieties that replaced them.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. Only 1 is correct. Statement 2 is false: in most states the extraction rate is greater than the rate of replenishment. Statement 3 is false: the high-yielding varieties of wheat and paddy needed more water than the traditional seeds.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Write a short situation about a farm in India whose soil became degraded and then recovered. It must use at least two of the traditional soil practices the chapter names. Then explain why the soil recovered.
questions.a: Any consistent situation, for example: a farm in Madhya Pradesh used heavy doses of chemical fertilisers and pesticides for years, and its crops grew poorer. The family then switched to cow-dung manure, covered the soil with mulch, and grew several crops together instead of one. Over a few seasons the crops improved. Explanation: improper use of chemicals had degraded the soil; natural fertilisers, mulching and multi-cropping are traditional practices that enabled holistic soil management, so the soil was replenished and rejuvenated.
s: A situation with soil degraded by improper chemical use
At least two traditional practices named by the chapter used correctly
Explanation of why the soil recovered

questions.q: Compare the groundwater problem and the soil problem described in the chapter, and analyse what stewardship requires for each. Cover: (a) the cause of each; (b) the effect of each; (c) the remedies the chapter gives for each; (d) what the two problems have in common; (e) one lesson the chapter draws from tradition.
questions.a: (a) Groundwater: extraction faster than the water table is replenished. Soil: the improper use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides. (b) Groundwater: a deficit that raises extraction costs and ends in unavailability, with many cities predicted to run out soon. Soil: degradation and crop failure. (c) Groundwater: water harvesting, rejuvenating ponds and tanks, cutting wasteful use, processing and reusing water. Soil: cow dung and other natural fertilisers, mulching and multi-cropping. (d) Both are renewable resources being pushed beyond their capacity to regenerate, so stewardship means using them only at a pace that lets them restore. (e) Traditional practice treated soil as part of Mother Earth and managed it holistically; the chapter says we must learn from such practices and apply them today.
s: Part (a): the cause of each
Part (b): the effect of each
Part (c): the remedies for each
Part (d): both are renewables used beyond regeneration
Part (e): the lesson from traditional practice

questions.q:
A city's water department reports (illustrative figures) that the city draws 900 million litres of groundwater a day, while rain and lakes recharge only about 600 million litres a day.
(a) What is the city's daily groundwater deficit?
(b) At this rate, how large does the deficit grow in a year of 365 days?
(c) Name two strategies from the chapter that would reduce the deficit, and say which side of it (extraction or recharge) each works on.
(d) Predict what the chapter says will follow if the city goes on drawing at this rate: name the stage that comes first and the stage that comes last.
questions.a: (a) 900 - 600 = 300 million litres a day. (b) 300 x 365 = 1,09,500 million litres in a year. (c) Any two, for example: rainwater harvesting or rejuvenating ponds and tanks (raise recharge); cutting wasteful use or processing and reusing water (reduce extraction). (d) The deficit builds up, which first raises the cost of extracting groundwater; the last stage is that the groundwater becomes unavailable, and the chapter predicts that many growing cities will run out of groundwater soon.
s: Part (a): 300 million litres a day
Part (b): 1,09,500 million litres a year
Part (c): two strategies, each linked to recharge or extraction
Part (d): higher cost of extraction first, unavailability last

questions.q: A cement factory runs beside a village in Andhra Pradesh. Which set of effects matches what the chapter says cement production causes?
questions.a: Dust harms lungs, cuts crop yields and pollutes soil and water. Its fine dust harms lungs and lowers crop yields, and it pollutes soil and water: the chapter says the dust enters the lungs of people and animals, settles on leaves and decreases yields, and causes soil and water pollution. It does not say the dust fertilises crops, that only factory workers are harmed, or that the only harm is noise.
o: Dust harms lungs, cuts crop yields and pollutes soil and water
Dust harms lungs but leaves plants, soil and water untouched
Dust settles on leaves and cuts yields, but does not reach lungs
Dust pollutes soil and water, but the air around stays clean

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the idea from the chapter in Column B.
Column A: 1. Sunshine-rich countries pool money and expertise for solar projects  2. A farmer grows certain plants together to keep pests away naturally  3. A factory fits dust-control equipment to meet official rules for cement plants  4. A resident gives up a personal comfort so the whole street benefits
Column B: a. Vrikshayurveda's advice  b. lokasangraha  c. the International Alliance for Solar Energy  d. Central Pollution Control Board guidelines
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. Pooling for solar power is the solar alliance; companion planting against pests is Vrikshayurveda's advice; dust control under official rules follows the CPCB guidelines; giving up personal comfort for all is lokasangraha.

questions.q: The chapter quotes the Bhagavad Gita's idea of lokasangraha. Which action from a town in Gujarat best reflects it?
questions.a: An owner pays for dust filters so neighbours breathe clean air. A factory owner fits costly dust filters so that the whole neighbourhood breathes cleaner air: lokasangraha is the idea that everyone must transcend personal desires and act for the wellbeing of all. The other actions put personal comfort or profit first.
o: An owner pays for dust filters so neighbours breathe clean air
A family buys an air purifier only for its own bedroom
A trader stocks bottled water to sell in a drought at high prices
A resident runs a generator all night for personal comfort

questions.q:
Pema's family farm in Sikkim earned Rs 1,50,000 a year with expensive chemical inputs and mounting debts (illustrative figures). When the state promoted organic farming, the family switched to compost, neem-and-garlic pest repellents and several crops a year. Its income fell 25% in the first year, then rose to Rs 1,20,000, Rs 1,35,000, Rs 1,50,000 and Rs 1,80,000 in years 2 to 5, and stayed at Rs 1,80,000 afterwards. A neighbouring farm kept using chemicals and earned Rs 1,50,000 every year.
(a) What was Pema's income in year 1, and why, according to the chapter, did yields fall at first?
(b) Which two of the family's changes replaced bought chemical inputs?
(c) How far behind the neighbour was Pema's farm in total income after 5 years?
(d) In which year did Pema's running total overtake the neighbour's, and what gain besides income does the chapter report for Sikkim?
questions.a: (a) Rs 1,50,000 less 25% = Rs 1,12,500; the soil was recovering from years of chemical use. (b) Compost replaced chemical fertiliser and neem-and-garlic repellents replaced chemical pesticide. (c) Pema's 5-year total: 1,12,500 + 1,20,000 + 1,35,000 + 1,50,000 + 1,80,000 = Rs 6,97,500; neighbour: Rs 7,50,000; behind by Rs 52,500. (d) Year 7: she gains Rs 30,000 a year over the neighbour, so the gap goes from -52,500 to -22,500 in year 6 and to +7,500 in year 7. Besides income, local biodiversity flourished (and tourism increased).
s: Part (a): Rs 1,12,500; the soil was recovering from years of chemical use
Part (b): compost for fertiliser and neem-and-garlic repellents for pesticide
Part (c): Rs 52,500 behind after 5 years
Part (d): year 7; biodiversity flourished or tourism increased

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mud is one of the traditional materials being revived to reduce the pollution caused by cement.
Reason (R): Buildings made of mud cannot last more than a few decades.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The chapter lists stone and mud among the traditional materials being used to reduce pollution. R is false: the chapter shows Jaisalmer fort, a mud structure built in the 12th century (later refurbished using sandstone), and a modern community building in Auroville made of mud using special techniques.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
The panchayat of a village in Andhra Pradesh measured the effects near a cement factory (illustrative figures).
| Place | Paddy yield per acre | Clinic visits for breathing trouble per 1,000 people a year |
| Fields within 500 m of the factory | 14 quintals | 85 |
| Fields 5 km away | 20 quintals | 30 |
(a) By what percentage is the near-field yield lower than the far-field yield?
(b) Which two effects of cement production named by the chapter do the two columns match?
(c) Besides air pollution, what other pollution does the chapter say cement production causes?
(d) Predict what the Central Pollution Control Board's guidelines, if the factory followed them, should do to the near-field figures, and name the chapter statement that supports your prediction.
questions.a: (a) (20 - 14) / 20 = 30 per cent lower. (b) Dust settling on leaves and decreasing yields (the yield column); fine dust entering lungs and damaging them (the clinic-visits column). (c) Soil and water pollution. (d) The near-field yield should rise and the clinic visits fall, because the guidelines aim to ensure that pollution is minimised or eliminated, and the harm the chapter describes comes from the dust.
s: Part (a): 30 per cent
Part (b): leaf dust cuts yields; dust in lungs damages them
Part (c): soil and water pollution
Part (d): yield up and visits down, since guidelines aim to minimise or eliminate pollution

questions.q: A farmer in Kerala follows a traditional recommendation and grows maize, beans and pumpkin together in one field instead of maize alone. She is growing ___ different crops together.

The chapter says traditional materials and methods combined with modern technology make new materials that are sustainable.
(a) Give two features that make such a material sustainable.
(b) Using (a), which of these features would most help a town whose main worry is unemployment, and why?
questions.a: (a) Any two: the production process is less polluting; it provides local employment; it is designed with the climate of the place in mind. (b) Providing local employment, because the material is made by people in the area, which creates work for them.
s: Part (a): two correct features
Part (b): local employment, with the reason

questions.q: True or False? 'Once a country starts switching to renewable energy, it no longer needs to be careful about how it uses its non-renewable resources.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says we must make the switch to renewables for as many purposes as we can, but non-renewables still have to be used so that they last long enough for humanity to find more sustainable alternatives; judicious use stretches them over a longer period.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: non-renewables must still be used judiciously so they last until alternatives exist

questions.q:
(a) What kind of countries does the International Alliance for Solar Energy (IASE), launched by India and France in 2015, bring together?
(b) Using (a), explain why the chapter says the alliance stands for both environmental responsibility and economic opportunity for Indians.
questions.a: (a) A coalition of sunshine-rich countries, focusing on countries with abundant sunlight throughout the year, committed to harnessing solar power. (b) Responsibility: solar power is a renewable source, part of the switch away from non-renewables. Opportunity: India has helped channel billions of dollars into solar projects across developing nations, sharing technical expertise and creating affordable financing, and parks like Bhadla show a country moving to renewable energy.
s: Part (a): sunshine-rich countries harnessing solar power
Part (b): renewable switch as responsibility; investment, expertise and financing as opportunity

questions.q: A builder in Tamil Nadu wants to put up a school while using as little cement as possible. Which choice follows the alternatives the chapter describes?
questions.a: Mud built with special techniques, stone, or blocks of recycled waste plastic. Walls of mud built with special techniques, or of stone: the chapter lists traditional materials such as stone and mud, new plant-based materials and recycled materials from waste plastic as the move away from polluting cement. More cement with a taller chimney, or importing cement, does not reduce its use.
o: Mud built with special techniques, stone, or blocks of recycled waste plastic
Cement from a factory with a taller chimney to scatter the dust
Fresh plastic sheets used in place of cement
More cement mixed with extra water so that less is needed

questions.q:
(a) Using the chapter's remarks, give one example from a city of unfair access to a basic resource.
(b) The chapter refers to lokasangraha. What would it ask of the owner of a factory whose fumes trouble nearby residents who cannot protect themselves?
questions.a: (a) Many areas of cities do not receive an adequate and regular supply of drinking water; or, air pollution from industries and fossil fuels affects those unable to protect themselves. (b) Lokasangraha asks everyone to transcend personal desires and act for the wellbeing of all; the owner should therefore cut the fumes even at a cost to his own profit.
s: Part (a): an example from the chapter, such as irregular drinking water or air pollution
Part (b): act for the wellbeing of all, not personal gain, by cutting the fumes

questions.q: A farm in Punjab suffers from over-pumped groundwater, chemicals in its well water and tired soil. Using only measures named in the chapter, suggest one change for the water, one for the pests and one for the soil.
questions.a: Water: harvest rainwater or rejuvenate ponds and tanks, cut wasteful use, or process and reuse water. Pests: use natural repellents, as the Sikkim family did with neem and garlic, and grow plants together that keep pests away. Soil: use cow dung, compost or other natural fertilisers, mulching and multi-cropping.
s: A water measure named in the chapter
A pest measure that replaces chemical pesticide
A soil measure that replaces chemical fertiliser

questions.q: 'Stewardship of natural resources is not only about the environment; it is also about fairness.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: (1) Access to basic resources such as water and clean air is often unfair to some sections of society. (2) In cities, many areas do not receive an adequate and regular supply of drinking water. (3) Air pollution caused by industries and excessive use of fossil fuels affects those who are unable to protect themselves from these hazards. (4) The chapter asks us to act as stewards of natural resources toward restoration, regeneration and sustainability, which covers everyone's share and not only one's own. (5) It closes with lokasangraha, the idea that everyone must transcend personal desires and act for the wellbeing of all. So stewardship asks who gets resources and who bears the harm, not only how much is used.
s: Unfair access to basic resources
Uneven drinking water in cities
Pollution hitting those unable to protect themselves
Acting as stewards toward restoration, regeneration and sustainability
Lokasangraha: acting for the wellbeing of all

questions.q: Kavya says: 'Vrikshayurveda shows that traditional knowledge alone can solve farming's problems today, so modern technology is not needed.' Is she right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that Vrikshayurveda holds elaborate sustainable advice: plants suited to each soil, irrigation by species and season, natural pest repellents, crop rotation and mixed cropping. She goes too far with 'alone' and 'not needed': the chapter speaks of learning from traditional practices and applying them in our current situation, and says traditional materials and methods are being combined with modern technological advances.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: its recommendations support sustainable farming
Wrong part: the chapter combines tradition with modern technology, so 'alone' overstates

questions.a: (a) Pest management through natural repellents and plants that should be grown together. (b) Crop rotation and mixed cropping to maintain soil health. (c) Proper methods of ploughing that retain soil moisture and let fungi, bacteria and earthworms grow. (d) Any one: methods of seed collection, preservation, or pre-planting treatments. (e) Vriksha means tree and ayurveda means the science of life or health, so it is a science of the care of plants and trees.
s: Part (a): natural repellents and plants grown together
Part (b): crop rotation and mixed cropping
Part (c): proper ploughing that retains moisture and soil life
Part (d): seed collection, preservation or pre-planting treatment
Part (e): tree plus science of life or health

questions.q:
Read the statements about sustainable practices and fair access.
1. Cement-making releases fine dust that settles on the leaves of plants and decreases their yields.
2. Jaisalmer fort, a mud structure of the 12th century later refurbished using sandstone, is shown in the chapter among traditional materials in use.
3. Access to basic resources such as water and clean air is always fair to every section of society.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says distribution and access, including to water and clean air, is often unfair to some sections of society.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: Write a situation set in an Indian city that shows unfair access to a basic resource. Name the resource, say who is affected, and say what the chapter shows about why they are affected.
questions.a: Any consistent situation, for example: in a Chennai ward on the city's edge the municipal pipe supplies water for an hour every second day, while the central colonies get it daily. The resource is drinking water; the residents of the edge ward are affected. The chapter says that in cities many areas do not receive an adequate and regular supply, and that access to basic resources is often unfair to some sections of society.
s: A situation naming a basic resource and a place
Says who is affected
Links to the chapter's point that access is often unfair to some sections

questions.q: In an industrial city, smoke from factories and heavy traffic fills the air for weeks. According to the chapter, who is hit hardest by such pollution?
questions.a: Those unable to protect themselves from the hazards. Those unable to protect themselves from such hazards: the chapter says air pollution caused by industries and excessive use of fossil fuels affects those who are unable to protect themselves, which is why access to clean air is often unfair. It does not say everyone suffers equally or that factory owners or visitors suffer most.
o: Those unable to protect themselves from the hazards
Only the owners of the factories that cause it
Everyone in the city, to exactly the same degree
Mostly visitors who are new to the city's air

questions.q:
(a) Why does the chapter say non-renewable resources must be used so that they last as long as possible?
(b) Using (a), suggest two purposes in your school for which a switch to renewable energy is possible.
questions.a: (a) Non-renewables cannot be replenished at the rate we use them, so they must last long enough for humanity to find more sustainable alternatives. (b) Any two realistic purposes, for example: lighting and fans run on rooftop solar panels; heating water for the canteen with solar heaters.
s: Part (a): they must last until sustainable alternatives are found
Part (b): two realistic purposes that renewables can serve
